title: Weavers, gomasthas and the system of advances
body: Once the East India Company established political power in Bengal and the Carnatic, it set out to eliminate competition and ensure regular supplies of cloth. It appointed paid servants called gomasthas to supervise weavers, collect supplies and examine the quality of cloth. Under the system of advances, weavers who received loans to buy raw material had to hand over the cloth they produced to the gomastha and could not take it to any other trader. Many weavers leased out their small plots of land to weave full time. The gomasthas were outsiders with no long-term social link with the village; they often came with sepoys and peons and punished weavers for delays. The price the Company paid was very low, and the loans tied the weavers to the Company.

title: Getting a job in a Bombay mill
body: In the early twentieth century, the number of people seeking work in Indian mills was always greater than the number of jobs. Industrialists usually employed a jobber to get new recruits. The jobber was very often an old and trusted worker. He brought people from his own village, ensured them jobs, helped them settle in the city and lent them money in times of crisis. A former Bombay millworker later recalled that workers paid jobbers money to get their sons work in the mill, and that millworkers stayed closely tied to their villages, returning home for harvest and sowing with the mills granting leave. Over time the jobber began demanding money and gifts for his favours and controlling the lives of workers.
